difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring recognition of a self-selection effect: patients who seek out experimental treatments differ systematically from those who don't, so the raw survival comparison is misleading. Distractors explain one horn only or deepen the paradox.
stimulus: Patients at a major cancer center who enrolled in experimental drug trials had a 12 percent higher five-year survival rate than patients at the same center who received only standard treatments. Yet when the hospital began offering the experimental drugs to all eligible patients, the overall five-year survival rate did not improve.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drugs used in the trials were considerably more expensive than standard treatments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who voluntarily enrolled in drug trials tended to be younger and in better overall health than those who did not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cancer center expanded its clinical trial program the same year it began offering experimental drugs to all eligible patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some patients who were offered the experimental drugs declined them and continued with standard treatments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Experimental drug trials at other hospitals showed similarly high survival rates among enrolled patients.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees were already younger and healthier, their higher survival rate reflects pre-existing advantages, not the drug's efficacy. Extending the drug to all patients — including the older, sicker majority — would not replicate the same advantage, explaining why overall rates didn't improve. Classic self-selection confound.
explanations.A: Cost explains a barrier to access but does not explain why broad access failed to improve outcomes. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Identifies a self-selection confound: the trial group's superior survival was attributable to pre-existing health advantages, not the drug itself.
explanations.C: Expanding the trial program in parallel is irrelevant to whether survival rates improved under broad drug access. Does not address the discrepancy.
explanations.D: Some patients declining the drugs would reduce uptake but does not explain why survival rates were unchanged even for those who did take them. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Consistent patterns elsewhere only confirm the paradox without resolving it — it deepens the puzzle by ruling out a center-specific anomaly.

difficultyReason: Policy paradox with a reverse-causation structure: the apparent protective effect of a policy disappears when causal direction is examined. Distractors offer plausible-sounding but incomplete explanations.
stimulus: Cities that adopted strict rent-control ordinances in the 1990s had significantly lower rates of resident displacement over the following decade than cities without such ordinances. Yet economists who studied the same period found that rent control did not, on average, reduce displacement rates in the cities that adopted it.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent control ordinances are typically accompanied by other tenant-protection measures that independently reduce displacement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cities that adopted rent control in the 1990s were, on average, already experiencing lower displacement pressures before the ordinances took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landlords in rent-controlled cities sometimes converted residential units to commercial use, reducing the overall housing supply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economists' studies relied on different displacement metrics than those used in the cross-city comparison.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rent control ordinances vary considerably in their specific provisions from one city to another.

explanations.correct: If cities that adopted rent control already had lower displacement pressures before the ordinances, the cross-city comparison reflects pre-existing conditions rather than the policy's effect. Within those cities, rent control still added nothing — consistent with the economists' finding. This dissolves the paradox via a pre-selection confound.
explanations.A: Companion measures could explain lower displacement, but then rent control itself is still doing no work — this would deepen rather than resolve the economists' finding that rent control specifically didn't help.
explanations.B: Correct. Pre-existing lower displacement rates explain the cross-city difference without crediting rent control, reconciling both findings.
explanations.C: Unit conversion would tend to worsen displacement, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.D: Different metrics could create an appearance of disagreement, but the stimulus contrasts raw rates vs. economist findings — a definitional mismatch that doesn't explain the underlying data discrepancy.
explanations.E: Variation in provisions might explain inconsistent effects but does not account for why rent-control cities as a group showed lower displacement. Resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: Environmental science paradox requiring identification of a confounding temporal variable. The student must recognize that baseline conditions differ between the two observed periods, not just compare the two stated outcomes.
stimulus: A coastal wetland restoration project replanted native marsh grasses across 400 hectares. Water quality measurements taken immediately after planting showed no improvement over pre-restoration levels. Yet five years later, water quality in the same wetland had improved substantially compared to similar, unrestored wetlands in the region.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the surprising phenomenon described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Native marsh grasses require several years to establish root systems capable of filtering significant quantities of pollutants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The restoration project also included installation of sediment barriers along the wetland's northern boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water quality in unrestored regional wetlands declined sharply over the same five-year period due to increased agricultural runoff.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The funding agency required water quality measurements immediately after planting as a condition of the grant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several migratory bird species returned to the restored wetland within two years of the planting project.

explanations.correct: If grasses need years to develop filtration capacity, the immediate absence of improvement is expected — the mechanism simply hadn't activated yet. The later substantial improvement is then fully explained. Both horns of the paradox are dissolved by this temporal lag.
explanations.A: Correct. The temporal lag between planting and filtration capacity directly explains both the immediate non-improvement and the later substantial improvement.
explanations.B: Sediment barriers might contribute to later improvement, but this leaves unexplained why there was no immediate improvement from barriers that were installed at the same time. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: If unrestored wetlands declined, the restored wetland's comparative improvement could reflect others getting worse rather than it getting better. This is a possible confound for the five-year comparison, but it doesn't explain the immediate non-improvement. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: The funding requirement explains why measurements were taken but not why they showed no improvement. Irrelevant to the substance of the paradox.
explanations.E: Bird return is a downstream ecological indicator and does not address water quality mechanisms at all. Irrelevant.

difficultyReason: Economics paradox involving a composition fallacy — aggregate data obscures a subgroup reversal. Recognizing that two distinct populations are being merged requires careful reasoning about measurement scope.
stimulus: A nationwide survey found that workers who regularly telecommute report higher job satisfaction than workers who commute to an office every day. Yet companies that shifted their entire workforce to mandatory remote work saw no increase — and often a decrease — in overall employee satisfaction scores.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who telecommute voluntarily tend to have jobs that are particularly well-suited to remote work and personal circumstances that make working from home advantageous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mandatory remote work policies are more common in large corporations than in small businesses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Job satisfaction surveys typically measure satisfaction along multiple dimensions, including compensation and career advancement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some employees who were required to work remotely lacked adequate home office equipment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Employee satisfaction scores at companies with mandatory remote work declined most sharply in the first six months of implementation.

explanations.correct: Voluntary telecommuters are a self-selected group whose jobs and home situations are favorable to remote work. They report higher satisfaction because of those pre-existing advantages, not because remote work inherently raises satisfaction. Forcing all workers — including those with unsuitable jobs or home situations — into remote work removes the selection advantage, explaining why mandatory policies don't raise and often lower satisfaction.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies the self-selection confound: voluntary remote workers differ systematically from the general workforce, dissolving the paradox.
explanations.B: Company size is irrelevant to the core mechanism of why voluntary vs. mandatory remote work produces different satisfaction outcomes.
explanations.C: Multi-dimensional surveys would apply equally to both comparisons and so cannot explain the divergent results. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: Equipment shortages partially explain some dissatisfaction but do not explain why satisfaction doesn't rise for employees who do have adequate equipment. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: The timing of dissatisfaction only specifies when mandatory remote work hurt satisfaction; it doesn't explain why voluntary telecommuters showed higher satisfaction in the first place. Resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: Technology paradox with a measurement-artifact resolution. The two data points use incompatible reference classes, so apparent inconsistency dissolves once the definitional mismatch is recognized.
stimulus: A cybersecurity firm reported that companies using its advanced intrusion-detection software experienced 40 percent fewer confirmed data breaches last year than companies without it. Nevertheless, an independent audit found that companies using the software suffered more total data security incidents than comparable companies without it.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cybersecurity firm's software is significantly more expensive than competing products on the market.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The software detects and logs minor unauthorized access attempts that would go unnoticed — and therefore unreported — at companies lacking such detection capability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Companies that purchase advanced intrusion-detection software tend to store more sensitive data than companies that do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Data breach notification laws require companies to disclose only breaches that result in the theft of personal information.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The independent audit was commissioned by a competitor of the cybersecurity firm.

explanations.correct: The firm reports fewer confirmed data breaches (serious, successful intrusions), while the audit counts total security incidents (including minor, detected attempts). The software reveals incidents that would otherwise go undetected and unreported, inflating the total-incident count. Both findings are thus consistent: the software reduces serious breaches while increasing recorded incidents by detecting previously invisible minor ones.
explanations.A: Cost is irrelevant to reconciling breach and incident rates. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. The definitional mismatch between 'confirmed breaches' and 'total incidents' is resolved by recognizing the software surfaces minor events that would otherwise be invisible, inflating the incident count without reflecting worse actual security.
explanations.C: Storing more sensitive data makes these companies more attractive targets and might explain more attacks, but it would predict more breaches too — deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.D: Disclosure laws affect reporting of breaches, not the total incident count measured by the audit. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Audit sponsorship is irrelevant to the content of the findings and does not reconcile the two data points. Irrelevant.

difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox requiring a hidden-mechanism explanation. The student must identify why a usage pattern diverges between naturalistic and experimental settings — a contextual confound that takes careful reading to isolate.
stimulus: Linguistic studies consistently show that bilingual children switch between their two languages — a phenomenon called code-switching — far more frequently when speaking informally with family than when speaking with peers at school. Yet in controlled laboratory settings, the same children code-switch at nearly identical rates regardless of whether they are speaking with a researcher who is also a family member or one who is a stranger.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Code-switching is considered a mark of bilingual fluency rather than a sign of language confusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children who code-switch frequently in informal settings tend to have larger total vocabularies across both languages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The formal laboratory environment itself suppresses the children's natural speech patterns, neutralizing context effects that would otherwise produce different rates of code-switching.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Schools in bilingual communities often have explicit policies discouraging code-switching in the classroom.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Children who spoke with researcher family members in the lab had met those researchers on fewer than three prior occasions.

explanations.correct: In natural settings, context (home vs. school) drives large differences in code-switching. In the lab, the formal setting overrides the social relationship cue entirely, so both the family-researcher and stranger-researcher produce the same, artificially suppressed rate. This confounding effect of the lab environment explains why naturalistic and experimental findings diverge.
explanations.A: The characterization of code-switching as fluent is irrelevant to why rates differ across contexts. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Vocabulary size is a correlate of code-switching frequency but does not explain why the family vs. stranger distinction has no effect in the lab. Irrelevant.
explanations.C: Correct. The lab setting is itself a confounding variable that neutralizes the social-context effect, reconciling the divergent findings.
explanations.D: School policies explain why school rates are lower than home rates — consistent with the first finding — but do not explain why the lab shows equal rates regardless of researcher relationship. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: The number of prior meetings would affect familiarity but does not explain why the overall lab rates are equalized and suppressed. Does not address both horns.

difficultyReason: History/policy paradox requiring a reverse-causation resolution. The apparent protective correlation between a practice and a negative outcome inverts when the causal direction is examined.
stimulus: Historical records show that medieval European towns with larger permanent garrisons of soldiers had significantly higher rates of violent crime than towns with smaller garrisons. Yet contemporary accounts and modern historians agree that the larger garrisons were deployed specifically to reduce violence and maintain order.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medieval soldiers stationed in towns were frequently recruited from the same regions as the local population.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Towns that already had high levels of violence were precisely the ones that authorities chose to garrison with larger numbers of soldiers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larger garrisons required greater provisioning, which strained local economies and created resentment among townspeople.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some soldiers stationed in medieval towns engaged in criminal activity themselves, contributing to local crime rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historical records of violent crime in medieval towns were compiled primarily by ecclesiastical authorities rather than secular administrators.

explanations.correct: If authorities deployed larger garrisons in response to already-high violence, the correlation between garrison size and crime reflects the pre-existing violence, not any failure of the garrison. The deployment was a reaction to the problem, not its cause. This reverse-causation explanation reconciles the statistical pattern with historians' accounts of garrisons being intended to reduce violence.
explanations.A: Shared regional origins of soldiers and locals is irrelevant to the crime-rate correlation. Irrelevant.
explanations.B: Correct. Reverse causation: high-crime towns attracted large garrisons, so the correlation runs the opposite direction from causation.
explanations.C: Economic strain and resentment could cause crime, but this would mean garrisons actually caused the crime, contradicting historians' benign accounts and deepening the paradox.
explanations.D: Criminal soldiers partially explain elevated crime but leave unresolved why authorities described garrisons as crime-reducing. Deepens the paradox by implying garrisons were counterproductive.
explanations.E: Record-keeping methodology might affect accuracy but does not account for the systematic direction of the discrepancy. Irrelevant.

difficultyReason: Law/ethics paradox with a scope-difference resolution. The apparent contradiction between two legal outcomes dissolves once the different jurisdictional or definitional scopes are recognized.
stimulus: In a series of rulings, the appellate courts of a particular country consistently found that warrantless searches of individuals' digital communications did not violate constitutional privacy protections. Yet over the same period, civil juries in the same country routinely awarded substantial damages to plaintiffs who sued government agencies for conducting those identical searches.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appellate judges in the country are appointed by the executive branch, while civil jury members are drawn from the general public.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The constitutional privacy standard applied by appellate courts is narrower than the statutory privacy right codified in the civil tort law under which plaintiffs sued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Civil damages awards were frequently reduced on appeal to lower amounts than juries initially awarded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The volume of warrantless digital searches increased substantially over the period in question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the plaintiffs who won civil damages had also filed unsuccessful criminal suppression motions based on the same searches.

explanations.correct: The appellate courts applied a constitutional standard (narrower), while civil juries applied a statutory tort standard (broader). A search can be constitutional yet still violate a separate statutory privacy right, making both outcomes simultaneously correct under different legal frameworks. The definitional mismatch between two distinct legal standards resolves the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: The different selection mechanisms for judges vs. jurors might correlate with different outcomes, but mere institutional difference doesn't explain how both legal outcomes can be legally correct simultaneously. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Two distinct legal standards — constitutional and statutory — can yield different outcomes for the same conduct without contradiction. Definitional mismatch resolution.
explanations.C: Reductions on appeal do not eliminate the awards or reconcile the finding that both outcomes were legally valid. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Volume of searches is irrelevant to why different legal bodies reached different conclusions about the same type of search. Irrelevant.
explanations.E: Failed suppression motions confirm the constitutional finding but don't explain the separate civil damages awards. Resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: Arts/economics paradox with a hidden third-factor explanation. The student must identify that a variable correlated with both success and the outcome creates a spurious relationship.
stimulus: A survey of professional musicians found that those who had received formal conservatory training earned, on average, 30 percent less annually than professional musicians who were self-taught. Yet music industry analysts consistently report that conservatory training substantially increases a musician's likelihood of sustained professional employment.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conservatory-trained musicians are disproportionately employed in orchestras and teaching positions, which offer stable but lower salaries than the top-earning self-taught performers in popular genres.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cost of conservatory training leaves many graduates with significant debt that reduces their net earnings over time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Self-taught musicians often cite conservatory-trained musicians as artistic influences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Music industry analysts focus primarily on rock and pop genres when assessing employment trends.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conservatory programs have become more selective over the past two decades, admitting fewer students each year.

explanations.correct: Conservatory training channels musicians into stable, moderately-paid careers (orchestras, teaching) with high employment rates. Self-taught musicians face more precarious employment overall, but the top earners in popular genres skew the average income of successful self-taught professionals upward. Average income is thus lower for conservatory-trained musicians even though their employment stability is higher — both findings are simultaneously correct.
explanations.A: Correct. Genre and role channeling explains the income gap: stable employment in classical/educational roles pays less than the highest-earning popular genre performers who are disproportionately self-taught among the employed. This reconciles both findings.
explanations.B: Debt reduces net earnings but doesn't explain why gross annual earnings from employment are lower, and doesn't address the employment stability finding. Resolves one horn only.
explanations.C: Artistic influence patterns are irrelevant to the earnings and employment discrepancy. Irrelevant.
explanations.D: If analysts focus on pop/rock, their employment findings would favor self-taught musicians, deepening rather than resolving the paradox.
explanations.E: Selectivity affects the pool of conservatory graduates but not the income or employment dynamics described. Irrelevant.

difficultyReason: Environmental science/policy paradox with a temporal-scope confound. The two observations are both accurate but cover different time windows, and the student must recognize that a lagged mechanism makes both consistent.
stimulus: Following a ban on a particular industrial solvent, atmospheric concentrations of the solvent in the affected region dropped by 60 percent within two years. However, rates of the respiratory illness most closely associated with solvent exposure continued to rise for four years after the ban took effect before finally declining.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain why illness rates continued rising after solvent concentrations fell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The respiratory illness associated with solvent exposure typically takes several years to manifest clinically after initial exposure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industrial use of the solvent was replaced by a chemically similar substitute that also poses respiratory risks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The region's population grew substantially in the years following the ban, increasing the absolute number of people at risk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medical screening programs for the respiratory illness were expanded significantly in the same year the ban took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enforcement of the solvent ban was inconsistent during the first six months after it was enacted.

explanations.correct: If the illness takes years to develop after exposure, then cases diagnosed in the four years following the ban reflect exposures that occurred before the ban reduced concentrations. The disease pipeline was already filled. Once that cohort clears, rates decline — exactly as observed. The temporal lag between exposure and clinical manifestation dissolves the paradox.
explanations.A: Correct. A multi-year latency period between exposure and clinical manifestation explains why illness rates continued rising from pre-ban exposures even as atmospheric concentrations fell post-ban.
explanations.B: A substitute solvent would explain continued illness indefinitely, contradicting the eventual decline in illness rates described in the stimulus. Deepens one horn of the paradox.
explanations.C: Population growth would raise absolute case counts but the stimulus refers to rates, which are population-adjusted. Irrelevant to the rate paradox.
explanations.D: Expanded screening would increase detected cases without changing actual illness rates — this could explain apparent continued increase, but only if the stimulus were describing detected cases rather than actual illness rates. As a partial definitional artifact answer, it is less complete than A, which explains both the rise and the eventual decline.
explanations.E: Inconsistent early enforcement might extend solvent exposure slightly but cannot account for four full years of rising illness rates after a 60 percent concentration drop. Resolves one horn only.
